prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

We report the first scattered light detection of a dusty debris disk surrounding the F2V star HD 15115 using the Hubble Space Telescope in the optical, and Keck adaptive optics in the near-infrared. The most remarkable property of the HD 15115 disk relative to other debris disks is its extreme length asymmetry. The east side of the disk is detected to ~315 AU radius, whereas the west side of the disk has radius >550 AU. We find a blue optical to near-infrared scattered light color relative to the star that indicates grain scattering properties similar to the AU Mic debris disk. The existence of a large debris disk surrounding HD 15115 adds further evidence for membership in the Beta Pic moving group, which was previously argued based on kinematics alone. Here we hypothesize that the extreme disk asymmetry is due to dynamical perturbations from HIP 12545, an M star 0.5 degrees (0.38 pc) east of HD 15115 that shares a common proper motion vector, heliocentric distance, galactic space velocity, and age.

outputs.L1: We report the first scattered-light detection of a dusty debris disk surrounding the F2V star HD 15115, obtained with the Hubble Space Telescope at optical wavelengths and Keck adaptive optics in the near-infrared. The most remarkable property of the HD 15115 disk, compared with other debris disks, is its extreme length asymmetry: the eastern side is detected out to a radius of approximately 315 AU, whereas the western side extends to a radius greater than 550 AU. We find that the disk exhibits a blue optical-to-near-infrared scattered-light color relative to the star, indicating grain-scattering properties similar to those of the AU Mic debris disk. The existence of a large debris disk around HD 15115 provides further evidence for its membership in the Beta Pic moving group, which was previously inferred from kinematics alone. We hypothesize that the extreme disk asymmetry is caused by dynamical perturbations from HIP 12545, an M star located 0.5 degrees (0.38 pc) east of HD 15115 that shares a common proper-motion vector, heliocentric distance, Galactic space velocity, and age.
outputs.L2: We present the first detection in scattered light of a dusty debris disk around the F2V star HD 15115, observed at optical wavelengths with the Hubble Space Telescope and in the near-infrared with Keck adaptive optics. Compared with other known debris disks, the most striking feature of the HD 15115 disk is its highly uneven extent. Its eastern side can be traced to a radius of about 315 AU, while the western side reaches beyond 550 AU. We measure a scattered-light color from optical to near-infrared that is bluer than the star, suggesting dust-grain scattering behavior comparable to that seen in the debris disk around AU Mic. The presence of a substantial debris disk around HD 15115 provides additional support for its association with the Beta Pic moving group, a link previously proposed solely from kinematic evidence. We propose that the disk’s pronounced asymmetry may result from gravitational disturbances caused by HIP 12545, an M-type star located 0.5 degrees, or 0.38 pc, east of HD 15115, and sharing the same proper-motion direction, heliocentric distance, Galactic space velocity, and age.

The study presents the first detection of scattered light from a dusty debris disk surrounding the F2V star HD 15115. This detection was achieved using a combination of Hubble Space Telescope optical observations and Keck near-infrared adaptive optics imaging. Together, these observations reveal the structure and scattering properties of the circumstellar material around the star, providing an important new example of a young debris disk system.

One of the most striking features of the HD 15115 debris disk is its extreme length asymmetry. The disk extends to approximately 315 AU on the eastern side of the star, while on the western side it can be traced to distances greater than 550 AU. This pronounced imbalance makes the disk highly unusual when compared with many other known debris disks, which often appear more symmetric in their large-scale structure.

The disk also displays a blue scattered-light color from optical to near-infrared wavelengths when compared with the stellar spectrum. This means that the dust grains scatter shorter wavelengths more efficiently than longer wavelengths. Such a color suggests that the scattering properties of the grains in the HD 15115 disk may be similar to those found in the debris disk around AU Mic, another young star with a well-studied dusty disk.

The discovery of a large debris disk around HD 15115 also strengthens the case that the star is a member of the Beta Pictoris moving group. This young stellar association contains several stars known to host prominent debris disks, including Beta Pictoris itself. The presence of a substantial disk around HD 15115 is therefore consistent with the star’s youth and with its proposed membership in this group.

To explain the disk’s remarkable asymmetry, the authors suggest that HD 15115 may have experienced dynamical perturbations from the nearby M-type star HIP 12545. A close gravitational interaction with this neighboring star could have disturbed the distribution of dust and planetesimals in the disk, stretching or truncating one side more strongly than the other. While this hypothesis requires further investigation, it offers a plausible explanation for the unusual one-sided structure observed in the HD 15115 debris disk.

The study presents the first detection of optical and near-infrared scattered light from the dusty debris disk surrounding HD 15115, an F2V star thought to be a member of the young Beta Pictoris moving group. Using high-contrast observations from the Hubble Space Telescope and the Keck Observatory adaptive optics system, the authors directly image starlight reflected by circumstellar dust grains and reveal the detailed structure of the disk. These observations provide important new constraints on the distribution, composition, and dynamical state of the material orbiting the star.

The disk is found to be remarkably asymmetric. On the eastern side of HD 15115, the scattered-light disk can be traced to a projected distance of approximately 315 AU, while on the western side it extends to more than 550 AU. This strong east-west imbalance is unusual among debris disks and suggests that the system has been dynamically disturbed. The disk also appears narrow and highly inclined, indicating that it is viewed nearly edge-on from Earth. Such a geometry makes the large-scale asymmetry especially striking, because the two opposing extensions of the same disk can be compared directly.

The color of the scattered light is another key result. The disk appears relatively blue, meaning that it reflects shorter optical wavelengths more efficiently than longer near-infrared wavelengths. This behavior is similar to that observed in the debris disk around AU Microscopii, another young star with a well-studied dusty disk. Blue scattering typically suggests the presence of small dust grains, which are efficient at scattering shorter-wavelength light. Because small grains are strongly affected by radiation pressure, stellar winds, and gravitational perturbations, their distribution can provide clues to the recent dynamical history of the system.

The results support the proposed membership of HD 15115 in the Beta Pictoris moving group, a nearby association of young stars with ages of roughly tens of millions of years. This is significant because young systems are expected to retain substantial amounts of debris produced by collisions among planetesimals, and their disks can preserve evidence of ongoing planet formation or dynamical evolution. The similarity between HD 15115’s disk and other young debris disks strengthens the case that the star belongs to this group.

To explain the extreme asymmetry, the authors consider the possibility that the disk has been perturbed by an external object. One plausible perturber is the nearby M-type star HIP 12545, which may have passed close enough to HD 15115 to gravitationally disturb the outer disk. Such an encounter could stretch or truncate the distribution of small grains, producing the observed lopsided structure. While additional observations and dynamical modeling are needed to confirm this scenario, the data indicate that HD 15115 is an important system for studying how debris disks respond to stellar encounters and other gravitational perturbations.

Overall, the study establishes HD 15115 as a striking example of a young, asymmetric debris disk seen in scattered light. The combination of Hubble and Keck imaging reveals a disk that is unusually extended, strongly one-sided, and composed of dust with blue scattering properties. These findings not only add HD 15115 to the growing sample of directly imaged debris disks but also provide valuable evidence for the dynamical processes shaping young planetary systems.

We report the first detection in scattered light of the debris disk surrounding the nearby F-type star HD 15115. High-contrast coronagraphic imaging with the *Hubble Space Telescope* at optical wavelengths, together with adaptive-optics observations from Keck in the near-infrared, resolves an edge-on, highly asymmetric circumstellar disk extending to several hundred AU. The disk is detected on both sides of the star, but the western extension is substantially longer and brighter than the eastern side, indicating a pronounced azimuthal asymmetry in the distribution of small dust grains. Comparison of the optical and near-infrared surface brightnesses shows that the scattered light is unusually blue relative to the stellar photosphere, suggesting a population dominated by small grains and/or non-standard dust properties.

The morphology and photometric properties of the disk are consistent with a dynamically young debris system. HD 15115’s kinematics support membership in the β Pictoris moving group, implying an age of order ∼10–20 Myr and placing the system among the young, nearby debris disks suitable for studying planetesimal-belt evolution. The extreme one-sided structure may reflect dynamical sculpting by an unseen planetary-mass companion, interaction with the local interstellar medium, or a recent gravitational perturbation. We note in particular that the nearby star HIP 12545 has a trajectory consistent with a possible close encounter, making it a plausible external perturber capable of exciting or distorting the HD 15115 disk. These observations establish HD 15115 as an important laboratory for investigating the early dynamical evolution of debris disks and the processes that generate large-scale disk asymmetries.

We report the detection of optical/near-infrared scattered light from the debris disk surrounding the young F-type star HD 15115. High-contrast imaging resolves the disk as a nearly edge-on, narrow structure with a pronounced bilateral asymmetry: the western extension is detected to substantially larger stellocentric radii than the eastern extension, giving the system a “needle-like” morphology unlike that expected for an unperturbed, axisymmetric planetesimal belt. The surface-brightness distribution and large radial extent indicate that small dust grains, produced by collisions among parent bodies and subsequently shaped by radiation pressure and dynamical perturbations, dominate the observed scattered light.

A plausible origin for the asymmetric structure is a recent or ongoing gravitational perturbation by the nearby star HIP 12545. HIP 12545 lies close to HD 15115 in space and has compatible kinematics, making a past close stellar encounter dynamically possible. Such a flyby could tidally disturb the outer planetesimal belt, preferentially stripping or exciting material on one side of the disk and producing the observed unequal extensions in scattered light. The direction and scale of the asymmetry are qualitatively consistent with a scenario in which weakly bound small grains, or their parent bodies at large radii, were displaced by the encounter. Although additional astrometric constraints and dynamical modeling are required to establish the encounter history uniquely, HIP 12545 remains a compelling candidate perturber for the unusual one-sided morphology of the HD 15115 debris disk.

## Research-paper summary: First optical and near-infrared scattered-light detection of the HD 15115 debris disk

The study reports the first resolved optical and near-infrared scattered-light images of a debris disk around **HD 15115**, a young nearby F-type star. Using high-contrast imaging, the authors detected an almost edge-on circumstellar disk whose scattered light reveals a strikingly asymmetric structure.

The disk is detected over a very large radial range. On one side of the star, the disk extends outward to roughly **550 AU**, while on the opposite side it is traced only to about **315 AU**. This strong east–west brightness and size asymmetry makes HD 15115 one of the more unusual debris disks imaged in scattered light, suggesting possible perturbations by unseen planets, interactions with the local interstellar medium, or past dynamical events.

A key result is that the disk appears **blue relative to the star** in optical to near-infrared colors. This means the dust scatters shorter-wavelength light more efficiently than expected for large, neutral-scattering grains. The blue color implies the presence of abundant small dust grains, likely comparable to or smaller than optical wavelengths, which are continually replenished by collisions among larger planetesimals.

HD 15115 is also important because it is associated with the **Beta Pictoris moving group**, a nearby young stellar association with an age of roughly **10–20 million years**. This connection places the system at an epoch when terrestrial-planet formation and planetesimal belt evolution are expected to be active. Along with systems such as **Beta Pictoris** and **AU Microscopii**, HD 15115 provides another resolved example of a young debris disk in the same moving group, making it a valuable laboratory for studying early planetary-system evolution.

Overall, the observations establish HD 15115 as a young, nearby, highly asymmetric debris-disk system with unusually blue scattered-light colors and a large radial extent, offering important clues about dust production, grain properties, and dynamical sculpting in young planetary systems.
